Vignette:
# Kofi's Vigil

Kofi Mensah had been a relief worker for five years before the ambush in South Sudan changed everything. At thirty-three, he had built a reputation as someone who could stay calm when systems collapsed—someone the NGO could count on to distribute medical supplies, organize shelters, document needs. In March of last year, he was in a compound near Bentiu with two colleagues and a driver when gunfire erupted without warning. The attack lasted perhaps three minutes. His driver was shot through the windshield. One colleague took shrapnel to the shoulder. Kofi was uninjured physically, but in those three minutes, he had come to believe something fundamental about the world: that safety was an illusion, that threat could materialize anywhere, at any moment, and that his ability to protect himself or anyone else was worthless.

The men responsible were never identified. No investigation was mounted. No one was held accountable. When Kofi returned to the United States two months later, he carried that injustice as a constant weight—not as a thought he could examine and release, but as a fact that had reorganized his understanding of how the world worked. What happened to him had been deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. The people responsible were still out there, unpunished, which meant they could do it again.

By his own account, Kofi had tried not to think about the event. When memories surfaced—the sound of glass breaking, the smell of cordite, the image of his driver's head tilting forward—he would push them away, detach from them, treat them as though they belonged to someone else's life. But the harder he pushed, the more his body seemed to remember. He startled at sudden noises. A car backfiring two months after his return sent him to the floor of his living room, his heart racing for twenty minutes afterward. His wife, Ama, found him there and said nothing, but her silence held a question.

At work, where Kofi managed social media for a nonprofit, his concentration had become unreliable. He would begin drafting a post about the organization's latest campaign and find himself unable to hold the thread of what he was trying to say. His mind would fragment. He would catch himself staring at the office window, scanning the street below, counting exits, noting which colleagues sat with their backs to the door. His supervisor had asked if everything was okay. Kofi said yes. He was not okay, but he could not explain that he no longer trusted himself to know when danger was coming. If he had failed to sense the ambush before it happened, how could he trust his own judgment about anything?

The hypervigilance had become his constant companion. Even at home, Kofi found himself alert in a way that exhausted him. He would lie in bed beside Ama, listening to the neighborhood—the distant sound of traffic, a dog barking, footsteps on the sidewalk—and each sound would register as a possible threat until he had categorized it and deemed it safe. This process happened automatically now, without his conscious intention. His eyes were always moving. His shoulders were always tense. Ama had stopped asking him to relax. She had stopped asking him much of anything.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was not a crisis but a quiet recognition: he was becoming someone he did not recognize. He had called in sick to work three times in two weeks, unable to face the open office. He had snapped at Ama over something trivial—a door left unlocked—and seen the hurt in her face. Most frightening to him was the sense that he could not trust his own mind anymore. He had always been capable, reliable, someone others depended on. Now he was certain that his judgment was compromised, that he might miss something crucial, that his own instincts would fail him when it mattered most. He came to his first appointment carrying that fear: that the person he had been before South Sudan was gone, and that whatever was left could not be trusted to keep anyone safe.
